# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

PRIMARY.missing: What I already do to cope (lip-reading, hearing aids or implants, asking people to repeat, phone caption apps like Live Transcribe, or captioning at the theatre) and how well that works. Could read captions while watching faces (Keel's suggestion: the glasses only help if they can keep their eyes on people while the words show) · Had their phone online -- with the box's bar reading 'Holds if no more than 1 in 3 say only sometimes, or no.'

screens.why1: Right after I've said how AirCaps fits their day (phone online), asking what it does better than their current way is the obvious next step in the solution walk.
screens.why2: The question and hint are plain to me, and they speak of deaf or hard-of-hearing adults and today's way in words I'd use myself, even if the example 'less time on it each week' is generic.
screens.why3: I know from our users and my co-founder's 20% at a table exactly what they get that lipreading, hearing aids and phone captions don't give them, so I can answer from what I know.
screens.why4: It is a free box of up to four lines with a single 'I'm not sure' escape, and that escape fits a founder who can't yet name a benefit.
screens.why5: The screen keeps my words exactly as typed, 'More of the talk followed without asking for repeats', and nothing is reworded.
screens.why7: The card asks for 1 to 4 benefits, each at most 9 words, naming what changes against today's way, with 'I'm not sure' as the founder's escape, and the box asks for exactly that; my single eight-word row is a noun phrase the belief can carry.

screens.why1: Right after I typed what AirCaps does better than today's way, Keel shows me the benefit back to check before it becomes the belief it tests, which is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: "More of the talk followed without asking for repeats" is a passive, clipped noun phrase I had to read twice; I'd say "following more of the conversation without asking people to repeat", and the belief's "would have given them more of the talk followed" reads even more awkwardly.
screens.why3: Losing the thread at a table with hearing people and having to ask them to repeat is exactly what my wearers live every week, and what the glasses are for.
screens.why4: The single row is the right benefit and distinct, but its wording is stiff and not how a deaf or hard-of-hearing person would put it.
screens.why5: It still means my benefit, following more without making others repeat, but the reword from my "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" has drifted toward awkward and lost the plain active voice.
screens.why7: One benefit in its own row, under 9 words, naming a gain today's way (hearing aids, lipreading, asking for repeats) does not deliver and that is true of the hard case; the belief carries it against the moment it went wrong (the last time they lost the conversation), with the 1-in-3 bar, so it can be supported or refuted.
screens.instead: Row: "Following more of the conversation without asking people to repeat"; Keel will test: "For most, with it, the last time they lost the conversation with hearing people, they would have followed more of it without asking anyone to repeat."

screens.why1: Right after what it fits into and what it does better, asking what they'll have to do to start is the obvious next question about my glasses.
screens.why2: Setup, extra steps, learning — plain words, and I answered it at once with wearing and charging.
screens.why3: I know exactly what my wearers have to do: put the glasses on in conversations and charge them daily.
screens.why4: The only option on this answer screen is the 'I'm not sure' escape, which fits an open box where the founder lists steps.
screens.why5: My own two steps are kept as typed and nothing of the product leaks into the question.
screens.why7: The box asks for steps the wearer takes themselves, up to four and at most 9 words, as the card wants, but the hint says 'setup, extra steps or learning' without naming a new habit of use, the hardest step the card's pitfalls say goes missing — my answers happened to be habits anyway.
screens.instead: What will they have to do themselves to start using it, and keep using it day to day? (setup, learning, or a new habit — up to four, each up to 9 words)

screens.why1: Right after I said what they have to do to start, it makes sense to read back the efforts Keel drafted before I pick one to test.
screens.why2: 'Wear the caption glasses in conversations' and 'Charge the glasses every day' are how my users and I talk; only the intro's echo of the title reads a little clumsy.
screens.why3: Both are things a deaf or hard-of-hearing wearer does themselves every week and can answer from their own routine.
screens.why4: The two rows are distinct and in my words, but the one-time setup every new owner actually faces, getting the app on their phone and pairing the glasses, is missing from the list.
screens.why5: The wearing row is my own as revised, and nothing of the team's side or the Pro plan leaks into the efforts.
screens.why7: Both rows are single base-form efforts in the wearer's own voice, under 9 words, within 1 to 4, neither a Compatibility or Purchase-friction condition, so a Yes or a No answers the belief.
screens.instead: Keep the two rows and add 'Set up the app and pair the glasses' (one-time, before first use), so I can choose between the setup hurdle and the daily wearing habit.

screens.why1: Right after I checked the efforts Keel wrote, picking which one is most likely to stop a deaf or hard-of-hearing adult is the obvious next step before the stranger's item.
screens.why2: 'Wear the caption glasses in conversations' and 'Charge the glasses every day' are plain words to me and to my wearers, and the title asks one thing.
screens.why3: I know from our power users and returns which of these two really holds people back, so I can answer from what I see every day.
screens.why4: Two distinct efforts, both mine and in my words, with no overlap; pairing to the phone is left to Compatibility, where it belongs.
screens.why5: Both rows are the efforts I typed, as revision 24 worded them, and 'Most would wear the caption glasses in conversations' still means what I meant: the real catch is putting them on in front of people.
screens.why7: Both rows are base-form efforts on the one measure, 'would they take this effort'; each is a step the wearer takes themselves, not a sign-off or a setup someone else does; neither repeats Compatibility or Purchase friction; and the belief, with its 1-in-3 bar, can be supported or refuted.

screens.why1: Right before the study goes out, asking whether to collect emails from people who want to try the glasses is exactly where a pilot offer belongs, and it ties to my 15-day risk-free returns.
screens.why2: "Pilot" is startup talk rather than how I'd say it to myself about a pair of caption glasses, though the hint's quoted line makes it clear on a second read.
screens.why3: Whether I want a list of deaf and hard-of-hearing people ready to try the glasses is my own call and I know the answer.
screens.why4: Yes or no is complete and distinct for this decision, and no escape chip is needed.
screens.why5: The respondent-facing line "Would you try this for real?" keeps the product out of it, but "try this for real" is vaguer than what I'd actually offer, which is ordering the caption glasses with free returns.
screens.instead: Ask the people who say yes if they'd like to try the caption glasses? They'd see: "Would you like to try this yourself? Leave your email." (Yes, ask them / No, don't ask)

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions belongs right before the study goes out, and the hint deals with my audience up front: every question is also written on screen and people can type or tap.
screens.why2: Plain to me: two named voices with a 5-second preview, a one-time recording cost of 400 credits either way, and the link sent by text.
screens.why3: As the founder I can judge which interviewer suits my study by tapping each preview, so it is fully answerable from what I know and do.
screens.why4: Daphne and Saskia are distinct, but for deaf respondents I would want a captions-first or text-only interviewer with no spoken voice, and the screen does not offer one even though most of my people will read rather than listen.
screens.why5: Nothing of AirCaps or the wearer role leaks here, and the hint keeps my audience's reading-first need in view.
screens.instead: Who should ask deaf or hard-of-hearing adults your questions? Options: Daphne (on video, every question captioned) / Saskia (on video, every question captioned) / Text only, no voice

screens.why1: Once the questions are set and the asker is chosen, choosing how my deaf and hard-of-hearing respondents will answer is the obvious next step before sending.
screens.why2: Each option says plainly what the respondent sees and does, and it states that Daphne's spoken questions are also written on screen, which is the first thing I'd check for my users.
screens.why3: I know how my wearers communicate: many read and type easily, some speak and some sign, so I can judge which format they would get through.
screens.why4: The three options cover voice-first, text-first and respondent's choice without overlapping, and Read and tap is the true fit for an audience that may not hear Daphne or whose speech a recogniser may mangle.
screens.why5: Nothing here alters my study or leaks the glasses to respondents, and it uses my actor wording, 'deaf or hard-of-hearing adults'.

screens.why1: Choosing who gets the link is the natural last step before sending, and it follows on from choosing who asks the questions and how people answer.
screens.why2: The choices are clear, but the 'Contacts page' has not appeared anywhere in my flow so far, and the second option switches from 'I' to 'you' partway through, so I had to read it twice.
screens.why3: I know who I would send to: the deaf and hard-of-hearing people I already know, the ones in our earlier user circle, plus groups like HLAA chapters or Deaf community pages where an open link would go.
screens.why4: The three channels are distinct and cover how I would reach people, but the second option is written partly in Keel's voice ('you send them') instead of mine like the other two, and it leans on a page I have not seen.
screens.why5: My pick of people I know by name is offered and kept, and nothing about the glasses or my roles leaks into this screen.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? -- People I know by name (I send each their own link) / People from a list I search for in Keel (Keel makes a link for each; I send them) / A group, with one open link (I post it where they already gather, like an HLAA chapter or Deaf community page; each person signs in with Google)

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right under the title with "3 beliefs: 3 holding · 7 people answered" beside it, and each card backs it with 7 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and by what count.
screens.why_b2: Each card says what was counted (said yes / would have gone better / would do it), over 7 people, against a bar of 5 of 7, so all three are plain at first look.
screens.why_b3: The three dimension names and the Compatibility and Adoption friction lines are mine, but the solution statement under the title is garbled ("the adult wearing the glasses the app on the lightweight glasses shows... and gets back live captions"), and the Relative advantage line is clumsy though still recognisable.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what holding means for AirCaps: whether to move to the commercial test, whether to watch the 3 who would wear the glasses only on a condition, or what that condition was.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible, but a unanimous 7 of 7 on three beliefs from seven people is presented with no word that this is a small sample, and nothing says how many of the people I sent the study to reached this stage.
screens.instead: Holding up on all three, but from only 7 people: 3 of them would wear the glasses only on a condition, so read that condition before you test the price, which is the next step.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside its deciding number, 7 of 7 said yes against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers over 7 people (4 easily, 3 most of the time, 0 against), and the strip puts the marker at 5 of 7, so what is counted, over how many and where the bar sits are all plain at once.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility and 'could read captions while watching faces' are the row I picked on the way in, in the words I checked.
screens.why_b4: The So line tells me this condition is not my blocker and sends me to Adoption friction, which is a concrete next place to look.
screens.why_b5: The count line keeps n=7 visible and calls it 'a lean, not a call', but the So line then says flatly that this 'is not what will stop them', which is firmer than seven hypothetical answers from people who have never worn caption glasses can carry.
screens.instead: So: none of the 7 expected trouble reading captions while watching faces. That is a lean from a small group answering hypothetically, so it is probably not the blocker; look at Adoption friction below.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 7 of 7 said it would have gone better against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The strip with my marker at 5 of 7 reads at once, but the chart line 'Better · 7 7 a lot · 0 a little' doubles the 7 and shows no against side, so I had to look twice to see it counts 7 people, all for.
screens.why_b3: Relative advantage is my dimension, and 'more of the talk followed without asking for repeats', set against the time they lost the conversation with hearing people, is the benefit I kept.
screens.why_b4: It tells me the advantage isn't my risk, and that the real question is whether they'd actually wear the caption glasses, which is Adoption friction, below.
screens.why_b5: Small n and the hypothetical are both flagged, but the question told strangers AirCaps is 'an app' when it is caption glasses, so seven 'a lot better' answers may be judging something closer to the phone captioning they already have, not my product.
screens.instead: Describe AirCaps in the question as caption glasses, not an app, and print the chart as 'Better 7 of 7 (7 a lot, 0 a little) · Not better 0'.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 7 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, with the 3 on a condition split out, so I know it held and by what margin.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the wear-the-glasses answers over 7 people, all 7 cells are for, and the marker sits at 5, so I see what is counted, over how many, and where the bar is at first look.
screens.why_b3: Adoption friction and 'Most would wear the caption glasses in conversations' are the step I picked, in my words.
screens.why_b4: The So line promises that what would make it worth it to those 3 is below, but the quotes don't deliver a next step: only Harriet's (borrow a pair for a matinee, check the lens under stage lights) points somewhere concrete, toward a trial or demo; Ruth's is about catching audience questions, and Tomás's says his end-seat workaround mostly works.
screens.why_b5: n=7 and 'a lean, not a call' are honest, but all three conditional answers share one condition, 'stays comfortable in conversation', which their own quotes don't say, and the So line claims the reasons are below when two of the three quotes are about something else, which is a soft overstatement.
screens.instead: Holding up, 7 of 7 (a lean on 7 people); 3 had a catch: Harriet wants to try the lens under stage lights before ordering, so offer a try-on or lean on the 15-day returns; Ruth's ask (audience questions in a big hall) is a pickup-range question, not effort; Tomás's end-seat trick mostly works, so his yes is soft.

screens.why_b1: The status word Holding up sits right beside 7 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b3: Adoption friction and 'Most would wear the caption glasses in conversations' are exactly the dimension and belief I checked.
screens.why_b4: The screen gives no next step: it never says to offer a try-before-you-buy at a show or to test whether the mics catch audience questions, even though the quotes point straight at both.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible and the 3 conditional answers are counted, but every quote is labelled 'Only if it stays comfortable in conversation for', which puts a comfort condition in the mouths of three people who said something else, and Tomás's quote describes a workaround that already works for him rather than any condition.
screens.why_b6: I did not type that stage lights might wash out the lens, that big-hall users need the audience questions picked up and not just the speaker, or that a one-sided user's end-seat trick already covers most of his week, and each one adds to what I wrote.
screens.instead: Held 7 of 7 (n=7), with 3 conditional: Harriet would buy after a borrowed matinee under stage lights and Ruth needs audience questions in big halls picked up, so test lens readability in theatres and far-field pickup. Tomás's end seat already works for him, so one-sided loss may be a weaker wedge.

screens.why1: As the first screen, it makes sense to check whether I talk with hearing people at all before asking about those conversations.
screens.why2: "Hearing people" is the phrase I use every day, and I can answer this the moment I read or hear it.
screens.why3: I know without guessing that I deal with hearing people at work, in shops and in my family every week.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it cleanly, and a gate correctly has no escape chip.
screens.why5: Nothing about the product leaks, but it drops "face to face", so I could say yes just from texting or emailing hearing people, which drifts from the founder's conversation-in-person focus.
screens.why6: It is short and easy to hear, but "I'll read 2 options" before a plain yes or no is clunky, and the guidelines say a screener should just end with "Yes or no."
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you talk face to face with a hearing person? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after asking if I talk with hearing people every week, it makes sense to ask whether I actually got lost in one of those conversations this past week.
screens.why2: I'd say 'lost track' or 'lost the thread' myself, but 'lose the conversation' is plain to me straight away, on screen or heard.
screens.why3: I know exactly whether I got lost at dinner or at a meeting table this week, since it happens to me all the time.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it cleanly, and the 'can't recall' and 'rather not say' chips belong to the story box after a Yes, not to this question.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product leaks to me, but 'at a table' narrows 'face-to-face, too fast or too noisy' to sitting at a table, so a week where I lost it standing in a noisy break room or at a party would have me saying No when the true answer is Yes.
screens.why6: Short, one question, 'Yes or no' at the end, easy to catch in one hearing.
screens.why7: The gate asks the thing that goes wrong (losing the conversation), not the routine of talking with hearing people, so someone whose week was all quiet one-on-one chats can truly say No and the share can hold or fail against the founder's band.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you lose track of a conversation with hearing people because it was too fast or too noisy? Yes · No

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I lost the conversation at a table with hearing people, showing me captioning glasses is the obvious next thing to show me.
screens.why2: Captions, lens, glasses and eye contact are all words I use every day, so I get it on the first read.
screens.why3: Losing eye contact when I look down at a captioning app on my phone is exactly my life, so I can picture this straight away.
screens.why4: It is a card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: This is an idea card shown on purpose, and it says plainly what it is, how it works and what they believe, in words I would use myself, so nothing leaks in a way it shouldn't.
screens.why6: Four short, plain sentences with no slashes, brackets or abbreviations, so they say well, though the second line repeats 'lightweight glasses' and 'inside the lens' from the first.
screens.instead: Imagine AirCaps, an app on lightweight glasses that captions nearby speech inside the lens. While people near you talk, their words show up in the lens as they say them. The people building it believe it would let you read the words while keeping eye contact.

screens.why1: Right after the AirCaps card, asking whether I could take in captions and faces together is plainly why it is asked.
screens.why2: The words are mine, but *last conversation* drops the *with hearing people* from the earlier screens, and *could you have read captions* makes me stop and wonder whether it means my phone's live captions or these glasses I have never worn.
screens.why3: In my last conversation at the table I had no captions in front of my eyes, so whether I *could have* read them while watching faces is a guess about the product, not something I did or know.
screens.why4: Yes, easily; most of the time; only sometimes; no reads as a fair ladder for something I could or could not do, and I can't tell fits as the escape.
screens.why5: It doesn't leak a company word, but it drifts from my existing habits toward the product's own selling point (captions in view while you watch faces).
screens.why6: It is short and is one question, and the four options are easy to hold when heard once.
screens.why7: The ability shape, the four rungs, the balance and the escape are all right, but the condition is really the idea's own benefit rather than something in how I already live that it must fit, so one rule is bent.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation with hearing people. Could you have kept glasses on through the whole conversation? Yes, easily; Yes, most of the time; Only sometimes; No; or I can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the captions question, asking whether it would have helped at the table where I lost the conversation is the obvious next thing.
screens.why2: The first half is my life in my words, but 'follow and join a face-to-face conversation' is stiff and repeats what 'lost the conversation' already said, so I would read it twice.
screens.why3: I know exactly the last dinner where I lost the thread and can judge whether captions in my glasses would have kept me in it.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference, worse, and I can't tell cover every answer I could give without overlap.
screens.why5: Calling it 'an app' drifts from the card's glasses that caption inside the lens, and 'follow and join a face-to-face conversation' reads like someone else's phrasing rather than mine.
screens.why6: The stem runs past twenty words with the long job clause in the middle, which is a mouthful to hold before the four short options.
screens.why7: One measure of better or not, the fixed four in order with No difference and Worse able to refute it, no benefit named, the hard case is the moment it went wrong, and I can't tell sits apart as the one escape.
screens.instead: Think of the most recent time you lost the conversation at a table with hearing people. Would AirCaps glasses have helped you keep up, or not? A lot better · A little better · No difference · Worse · I can't tell

screens.why1: After the idea and whether it would have helped, asking whether I'd actually put the glasses on is the obvious next thing to ask me.
screens.why2: Caption glasses and wearing them in conversations are plain to me on first reading or hearing.
screens.why3: I know whether I'd wear glasses at a table with hearing people, how they'd feel on my face and how people would look at me, so I can answer this from my own life.
screens.why4: The yes, the only-if, probably not and no are distinct and cover my true answers, and I can't tell fits as the escape, though 'comfortable' could mean on my face or socially, and both readings work for me.
screens.why5: It names the idea card's AirCaps and caption glasses and nothing more, with no founder terms for people like me.
screens.why6: It is one short question with four short options I can hold, and the escape is said last.
screens.why7: Wearing the glasses is a habit I take on myself, the options are the fixed four with yes and only-if for and the two noes against, the condition is specific to wearing glasses rather than true of every step, and I can't tell sits apart.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I'd wear the caption glasses, it makes sense to ask what would make them worth it to me, as the last thing before I go.
screens.why2: Short and plain, and it names AirCaps rather than leaving me a bare 'it' to work out, though it doesn't point back to what I said about wearing the glasses.
screens.why3: I've never used AirCaps, so I'd answer from what goes wrong for me at a loud table: keeping up with fast talk, knowing who's speaking, and not looking down while people look at me; that part is half guessing.
screens.why4: A box to type in, with no options.
screens.why5: It uses the name from the idea card and nothing new about the product or the people behind it, though 'worth it' could make me think about price when nobody has said one.
screens.why6: One short question that I'd catch on one hearing and could answer out loud.
screens.instead: What would the glasses have to do at a noisy table for you to keep wearing them?
